concept.shortExplanation: Once meaning is geometry, comparing two words becomes a distance calculation. Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and ignores their length, which is why it is the default choice — it asks whether two words point the same way, not how emphatic they are. Euclidean distance answers a different question and will rank things differently. Every number in this chapter is computed live from real embeddings.
concept.ahaMoment: Retrieval, search, recommendation and RAG are all this one operation at scale: embed everything once, then answer queries by finding the nearest angle. The whole retrieval industry is a dot product with good indexing.

levels.title: Rank by Similarity
levels.instructions: Drag the words into order, nearest to the anchor word at the top. Your ordering is compared against the real cosine ranking using rank correlation.
hints: Think about which words share the most real-world context with 'doctor' — same profession, same workplace, or no relation at all — rather than free-associating.

'Surgeon' is a specific kind of doctor, so it sits clearly closest. 'Bicycle' shares almost no context with 'doctor', so it belongs at the very bottom. Nurse, lawyer and hospital are all much closer to each other than to either extreme, so their exact order matters far less.
Rank, closest to furthest: surgeon first, then nurse, lawyer and hospital bunched together in the middle (in roughly that order), then bicycle clearly last.

levels.title: Odd One Out
levels.instructions: One word in each set sits furthest from the others in embedding space. Find it. The outlier is determined live by mean pairwise cosine similarity, not by a stored answer.
hints: In each set, three words share an obvious category and one doesn't belong. Find the theme first, then find what breaks it.
Set one is musical instruments, set two is planets, set three is metals — in each case there's exactly one word from a completely different domain sitting among them.
The odd ones out are: avalanche (not an instrument), diploma (not a planet), and sonnet (not a metal).

levels.title: Cosine vs Euclidean
levels.instructions: Bring your own words. Build a set of five, then predict which pairs the two metrics will disagree about. The heatmap recomputes live under both metrics as you type.
hints: Cosine only cares about direction; Euclidean also cares about length. The two metrics can only disagree about which of two words is 'closer' when the vectors involved have noticeably different magnitudes.

Mixing very common, short words (which tend to have smaller, more 'average' embeddings) with vivid, unusual or rare words (which tend to sit further from the origin) creates the magnitude gaps that make cosine and Euclidean rank pairs differently.

Build a set mixing plain function words (like 'the', 'is', 'a') with vivid, unusual ones (like 'photosynthesis' or 'kaleidoscope') — the magnitude gap between them is what produces disagreements for the heatmap to reveal. There's no single fixed set that works; any mix of 'plain' and 'unusual' words in this shape tends to.
